records.title: Reach, defense and recovery
records.markdown:
# Reach, defense and recovery

Ancestry traits use the ordinary action, targeting and recovery procedures together with their printed grants.

## Touch and object interactions

Ordinary physical reach extends to an adjacent square. A touch ability is one whose rules or narrative require contact with its target. An ability’s printed adjacency requirement describes distance; its description establishes whether it uses physical contact.

An explicit reach grant gives its printed distance for the interactions it names. Long Reach gives Tallfolk a range of 2 squares for object interactions and non-attack touch abilities. Use the ordinary action cost each time: picking up an object costs a Maneuver, and a touch ability spends its printed action and costs. Attack range follows the attack’s printed rules.

For example, a Tallfolk with Long Reach can pick up a key 2 squares away with a Maneuver, or use a healing touch ability on an ally 2 squares away. Each use follows its ordinary action cost.

## Defense Boons when the attacker rolls

When the defender rolls, apply defense Boons and Banes to that defense roll. When a player-controlled attacker makes the roll instead, each applicable defense Boon becomes 1 Bane to the attack, and each applicable defense Bane becomes 1 Boon to the attack. Combine those with the attacker’s own Boons and Banes normally.

For example, Small Target gives a gnome 1 Boon to defense rolls. Against an attack rolled by another player, that benefit instead supplies 1 Bane to the attacker’s roll.

## Oath-Bound recovery

Oath-Bound count as living creatures for healing and use the ordinary hero rules for HP, scars, rest and recovery.

## Paying HP costs

When an ability asks you to spend HP, pay its printed amount. This cost bypasses resistance and must leave you with at least 1 HP.

## HP unavailable for recovery

When an ability makes spent HP unavailable for recovery until a stated time, record that HP and its release time. During that period, healing and overnight rest can restore HP up to maximum HP minus the unavailable amount. Record this separately from scars and maximum HP.

For example, an Oath-Bound with maximum HP 20 uses The Debt Comes Due and spends 1 HP. Until the next dawn, healing or overnight rest can restore them to 19 HP. At dawn, that HP becomes available for ordinary recovery again.

A reroll replaces the original roll for the same action or event. Use the original attribute and applicable Boons and Banes, roll again, and resolve the new result, including its retained natural dice.

records.title: Conditions
records.markdown:
# Conditions

Shared condition rules.
Use these timing and sensory rules throughout the current catalog.

## Ratings, decay, and persistence

At the end of the affected character's turn, resolve a temporary numbered
condition's effect, then reduce its rating by 1. At 0 it ends. A condition gained
during that turn also decreases at that turn's end. Numbered instances add where
meaningful; binary states do not. Normal Boon/Bane cancellation and caps apply.

The number can describe severity as well as duration (Dazed, Burning), or duration
only (Blinded, Paralyzed). A higher duration-only rating does not strengthen the
condition. Dazed 3 or greater grants no action categories.

An asterisk means **no automatic decay**: Blinded 1* is blindness that persists
until its specified remedy. It does not mean every such injury is incurable.
The source states which remedy removes it.
Maintained Grappled does not decay. Binary conditions and lasting effects
use their own removal rules.

Spend a **Main Action** to reduce an appropriate condition on yourself or an
adjacent creature by 1 without a roll: staunch Bleeding, extinguish Burning, or warm
someone suffering Freezing with a plausible method. This is not a universal cure
for every condition. Specialist abilities can remove more or use a cheaper action.
A star prevents automatic decay, not a removal method explicitly allowed by its
source. Record temporary and starred contributions separately, using the mixed-source
tracking procedure below.

Example: untreated Bleeding 3 deals 3 damage, decreases to 2, then deals 2 and 1
on subsequent turns before ending. A Main Action reducing it before the first tick
changes that sequence to 2, then 1. Matching resistance can reduce a Burning or
Freezing tick to 0. Matching damage immunity also makes it 0. The condition
still decays normally. Immunity to the condition prevents it from applying.

## Temporary and lasting conditions

A temporary numbered contribution resolves and decays at the end of the affected
creature's turn. A starred contribution has no automatic decay. A lasting effect remains until its printed remedy. Maintained Grappled and binary Prone
instead use their own release, escape or standing rules.

An asterisk means persistent, not necessarily incurable. Follow the ability or hazard's remedy. Temporary Blinded 2 clears after two end-of-turn decay steps; Blinded 1* from a curse remains until that curse's remedy is met. Safe overnight rest restores HP but does not override that remedy. Scars apply no conditions.

## Condition reference

| Condition | Effect | Removal / persistence |
|---|---|---|
| Burning X | Fire X damage at end of turn. Fire resistance can reduce it to 0. | Resolve damage, then decay; appropriate Main reduces 1 |
| Freezing X | Cold X damage at end of turn. Cold resistance can reduce it to 0. | Resolve damage, then decay; appropriate Main reduces 1 |
| Bleeding X | X damage at end of turn, bypasses resistance | Resolve damage, then decay; appropriate Main reduces 1 |
| Poisoned X | X Banes to action/defense/death rolls, not inventory dice; no damage | Decay unless explicitly maintained or persistent |
| Frightened X | X Banes while its source is perceptible; no forced choices or movement | Decay unless explicitly maintained or persistent; source must be identified |
| Blinded X | Cannot see; use an explicit alternative-sense targeting grant where applicable | Duration only; decay; Blinded 1* requires its specified remedy |
| Deafened X | Cannot hear; cannot respond to hearing-only triggers | Duration only; decay; Deafened 1* requires its specified remedy |
| Slowed X | Speed −X, minimum 0 | Decay unless explicitly persistent |
| Dazed X | At 1/2/3+, choose 2/1/0 of Main, Maneuver, Reaction; movement remains | Choose at turn start; no retroactive change to spent actions; decay 1 at turn end |
| Grappled X | Movement 0; at 1/2/3+, choose 2/1/0 of Main, Maneuver, Reaction | Maintained. Force reduces 1/2/3 when a Main remains. At 3+, escape requires release or an outside intervention. |
| Prone | Crawl for 2 movement per normal square or 3 per difficult square, including diagonally | Spend 2 movement to stand, or end as the source specifies |
| Asleep X | Unaware, no actions/movement | Default numbered decay; adjacent Main wake effort reduces 1; damage ends it; source can specify persistence |
| Paralyzed X | Aware, no actions or movement at any positive rating | Duration only; decay; no gradual return of options before 0 |
| Unconscious | Unaware, prone, no actions/movement | Source; ordinary healing wakes only HP-caused unconsciousness |
| Petrified | Inert solid, unaware, no actions/movement | Source defines protection and cure |
| Hidden | Universal hidden state, not observer-specific | Ends on attack/open revelation; DA judges concealed movement |
| Invisible | Cannot be seen; not automatically unlocated | Source; attacking ends Hidden, not automatically Invisible |

Asleep, Paralyzed, Unconscious, and Petrified apply three defense Banes; overlapping
helpless states apply that penalty once. Dazed adds no defense Banes.
Attacks against a Grappled creature gain one Boon per level of its Grappled rating,
including attacks against grapplers, using normal Boon/Bane rules.
When Dazed and Grappled coexist, use the greater action restriction, not their sum.

Grappling restricts the grappler by their own contribution as well as the target.
Multiple grapplers' contributions add on the target. Each can freely release even
at rating 3, ending their contribution. An outside intervention can break a hold
by separating the grappler from the target beyond its reach or rendering the
grappler unconscious. A creature at Grappled 3 or higher can be
cuffed by an adjacent character using a Maneuver and suitable
[restraints](../equipment/restraints.md). Once the captive is secured and combat is
over, resolve the scene through ordinary narration.

Example: Paralyzed 3 prevents actions and movement, falls to 2 at turn end, then
to 1, then clears. Dazed 3 instead gradually returns action options as it decays.
Blinded 2 is full blindness for two decay steps, not stronger blindness than 1.

**Provisional prone combat rider for tests:** none beyond movement until approved.
Do not import automatic melee Boons or ranged Banes from another game's prone rule.

See [recovery](recovery.md) for HP and treatment and [foundations](foundations.md) for movement.

## Action-category timing — latest agreement

Dazed and Grappled determine retained action categories at the start of the affected
creature’s turn. Changes during the turn do not undo spent actions or recalculate
that turn’s category selection. Temporary Dazed decays at turn end; maintained
Grappled does not decay. Grappled’s movement restriction still applies while the
hold exists. Paralyzed, Asleep and Unconscious retain their immediate restrictions;
they are not action-category selection effects.

**Mixed-source tracking:** record temporary and starred contributions
separately. Add effective severity where the condition uses severity; decay only
the temporary part. For duration-only conditions, either positive contribution
keeps the condition active, without multiplying its effect. Generic temporary
reduction removes temporary rating only; permanent treatment follows its source.

records.title: Encounter budgets and CV calibration
records.markdown:
# Encounter budgets and CV calibration

**Agreed targets:** four player characters are the reference party; typical combat
about 4 rounds, hard about 6, extreme about 10. Typical reasonably prepared parties
should have roughly a 20–30% chance of at least one hero falling to 0 HP without a healer,
5–15% with one. These are feel targets, not mandatory outcomes for every battle.

## Proposed budget procedure

Define B(L) as the calibrated standard encounter budget for four characters of
level L. For N characters of the same level:

**Budget = B(L) × N / 4 × difficulty multiplier.**

Proposed multipliers: easy 0.75, standard 1.00, hard 1.50, extreme 2.00. Round the
final budget to a convenient whole CV. These multipliers are starting fixtures,
not verified mappings to encounter duration. An extreme encounter must not simply
be declared a ten-round fight because its budget doubled.

For mixed levels, use **sum(B(character level) / 4)**, then multiply by difficulty.
This preserves each character’s calibrated contribution rather than rounding the
party’s average level. Budget is the sum of participating enemies’ CV. Waves and
reinforcements count; terrain and mission objectives require separate review.

**Arithmetic example only:** if future calibration establishes B(1)=40, three
level-1 characters receive a standard budget of 30; five receive 50. A hard fight
for five would be 75. Forty is a demonstration input, not an assigned level-1 budget.

## Proposed creature estimate, followed by testing

Start with **CV estimate = sqrt(E × O) × U**, normalized so a chosen reference
creature has the desired reference CV.

- E = expected attacks needed to defeat it using the reference party’s actual
  attack outcomes, hit effects, resistances and relevant control. Do not divide HP
  by a single raw damage number that ignores minimum damage.
- O = expected effective HP damage per round against that party, counting actual
  targets, action economy and healing. Use recorded outcome probabilities and
  attack/defense attributes, not an assumed universal success rate.
- U = an explicit provisional adjustment for disabling effects, movement, unusual
  senses, reach, summoning or other advantages not represented by E and O. Start
  at 1 for an ordinary damage-only creature; document every other value.

This is a seed metric, not a final algorithm. Zero-damage controllers cannot receive
zero CV: evaluate their contribution in a mixed encounter instead of applying this
formula blindly. Healing loops, area attacks and incapacitation can make the simple
estimate unreliable. Record uncertainty rather than publishing false precision.

## Calibration sequence for the bestiary

1. Build a few ordinary melee/ranged creatures with full printed attack and defense
   attributes, HP, resistances, Stability, actions and outcomes.
2. Test actual level-1 parties with documented supplies and healing access.
3. Fit B(1) and creature CV to duration, falls to 0 HP, defeat risk and action loss.
4. Test 3-, 4- and 5-character parties and easy/hard/extreme multipliers. Include
   open and obstructed terrain; party-size scaling may need an enemy-count warning.
5. Add control, healing and summons one feature at a time; refine U or replace the
   seed metric if it fails. Then repeat at levels 3 and 7 and intermediate levels.

Until those tests exist, CV and B(L) remain uncalibrated. The procedure is ready to
support bestiary development; numerical encounter guarantees are not.

## Bestiary seed worksheet

The [bestiary encounter draft](../bestiary/encounters.md) now supplies explicit
reference attacks, enumerated probabilities, utility factors and a proposed
B(L)=32+8L testing grid. These are authoring seeds, not the completed calibration
described above. Every creature’s CV can be recomputed by the bestiary audit.

records.title: HOL foundations for authoring
records.markdown:
# HOL foundations for authoring

These summarize the approved system. Bruce resolves discrepancies; current
cards and rules are the source, not earlier editions.

## Resolution

Roll only for uncertainty with consequences. Correct fictional action may reveal a
clue without a roll. The DA asks for Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge or
Reason; the player takes an action which may call for that roll. Force is an action,
not another attribute or a separate skill-roll category.

Roll 3d6 plus one attribute. Weak is 8 or below: progress, not automatic success.
Standard is 9–14. Strong is 15 or above. Three natural retained sixes give Strong
plus a benefit; three retained ones give Weak plus a complication.

Boons and Banes cancel. Use at most three net extra dice, retaining the best or
worst three. Difficulty comes through Banes, never another target number on the
same roll. A cumulative task’s progress target is a different thing: 1/2/3 progress
per Weak/Standard/Strong result.

## Turns and attacks

At combat start, the DA decides whether either side has pulled off an ambush.
An ambushing side starts without an initiative roll. Otherwise, one player rolls
unmodified 3d6. On 12 or more, the players start. On 11 or less, the opposition
starts. The starting side opens every round.

Alternate sides from the first turn of combat. Each side chooses its next
character, and the side with turns remaining finishes them when the other runs
out. A round lasts 6 seconds and ends after everyone has had a turn. Each
character has Main, Maneuver, Reaction and movement. Main converts to Maneuver,
and Maneuver converts to movement. Conversion goes in that direction only.

Player attacks use one attacker roll, even against a player. NPC attacks use the
player’s defense roll. Strong defense receives Weak attack effects, Standard
receives Standard, Weak receives Strong. The defense itself spends no Reaction.
Players roll their controlled creatures’ printed attack and defense attributes.
For NPC-only actions, either a player or the DA assuming the player role rolls.
For an NPC-versus-NPC attack, roll the defender’s printed defense attribute and
read the attacker’s defense-outcome table. For consequential NPC healing or other
tasks, roll the acting NPC’s printed attribute and outcomes. Apply the ordinary
modifiers and use one roll; handling the dice does not transfer control of the NPC.
Off-screen events may be resolved by DA judgment without simulating combat.

Damage is fixed by the card. Remove components covered by damage immunity first.
Apply weakness, then the highest resistance of each remaining type, normally
capped at 3, then other reductions. An attack deals a minimum of 1 total damage
if at least one positive damage component survived immunity. Damage outside the
attack's immediate outcome, such as condition ticks, falls, and collisions, can
be reduced to 0. A fully immune event deals 0 HP damage. Conditions and other
riders follow their own rules.
Condition immunity prevents the named condition from applying. Use the explicit
immunities on the creature or granted by an effect.

Damage types are Physical, Fire, Cold, Lightning, Poison, Life, Radiant, Mental,
and Force. Current bestiary condition immunities are Asleep, Bleeding, Blinded,
Frightened, and Poisoned. A creature or effect can explicitly name another condition.

**Numerical weakness — approved October 16, 2026:** Weakness X increases the
matching damage component by X before resistance. Apply each weakness once per
damaging event. Use the highest applicable weakness of each type, not the sum of
multiple sources, with a normal cap of 3. A damaging effect must include that
type; weakness does not add an absent damage type.

**Example:** Fire Weakness 2 changes 3 fire damage to 5 before resistance.
An event dealing 4 physical and 1 fire instead becomes 4 physical and 3 fire;
an event dealing only 4 physical is unchanged. Apply matching resistances next.

Special vulnerabilities, such as fire stopping regeneration, use their printed
procedure. They do not imply numerical weakness or extra damage unless stated.

## Cover

The DA judges whether an obstruction protects the target from the attack. Partial
cover gives the attacker 1 Bane. Heavy cover leaves a narrow attack path and
gives the attacker 3 Banes. If the defender rolls, apply the same number as Boons
on that defense roll. Apply cover once to the roll being made, using the usual
Boon and Bane rules.

An attack needs a usable path. A barrier that blocks the path prevents the attack.
An attack that requires sight needs a visible target or an explicit alternative
that permits targeting. Follow the attack's printed targeting rules.

## Movement

Entering a normal square costs 1 movement and entering a difficult square costs 2.
While Prone, crawl for 2 movement per normal square or 3 per difficult square.
Use the same costs for straight and diagonal steps. Standing costs 2 movement.
You may cross an occupied square if its occupant is Prone. Pay the higher of 2
movement or your usual cost to enter it, and finish in a free square. Crawling is
voluntary movement and can provoke when you leave an
enemy’s melee reach. Forced movement consumes the entered terrain’s cost. Any
positive remaining budget can enter the final square and stop even if that cost
exceeds the budget.

Push X moves the target up to X squares directly away from the source. Pull X
moves it up to X squares directly toward the source. Slide X moves it up to X
squares in any direction, including vertically. The effect’s user chooses the
path for a Slide and can stop any of these movements early. A Push or Pull
changes elevation only if its effect allows it. Follow any restrictions in the
effect. Collision damage requires an actual impact.

Collisions gather movable creatures and intact movable objects into a group that
moves as one creature on the original remaining allowance. Each new impact deals
physical damage equal to the movement remaining at contact to every member of the
group and whatever it strikes. Creatures and objects with HP each apply their own
damage defenses. The DA judges the impact on objects without
HP. Remove any movable object that breaks, including one reduced to 0 HP. Then
deduct a newly struck creature’s Stability once for that movement. Continued
contact between group members deals no further damage.

A fixed barrier stops the group even if it breaks. Add 1 to the damage dealt to
each group member and the barrier before resistance. After placement, only the
original mover bounces one square opposite the impact. If that square is blocked,
the mover stays in place without another collision or damage.

**Group placement — approved October 16, 2026:** move the group along the forced
movement path and finish in separate legal spaces. If everyone cannot fit, stop
at the last position where they can. The DA determines the exact arrangement;
placement cannot pass through walls or grant extra forward movement.

All actors have [Stability](stability.md): default 0, explicit grants only, maximum
3, highest source. It consumes forced movement once per newly struck creature,
including through a collision chain; no protection against Prone or conditions.

## Conditions

Resolve a temporary numbered condition at turn end, then reduce by 1. Burning and
Freezing deal their rating in matching elemental damage; Bleeding bypasses
resistance. Poisoned applies its rating in Banes, not damage. Frightened supplies
Banes while the stated source is perceptible. Slowed reduces Speed.

Dazed 1/2/3 leaves two/one/no categories among Main, Maneuver and Reaction; choose
at turn start. Movement remains. Paralyzed stops actions and movement at any
positive rating; its number is duration. Blinded and Deafened numbers are duration,
not severity. An asterisk prevents automatic decay; a persistent binary sense loss
needs only rating 1*. Removal follows the source.

Grappled prevents movement and reduces action choices like Dazed; it is maintained,
not decaying. The grappler suffers their own contribution too. Force can reduce
Grappled while Main is retained. At rating 3 or higher, escape requires a grappler’s
release or an outside intervention that breaks the hold. Separation beyond reach,
unconsciousness, or death ends that grappler’s contribution. Attacks gain Boons equal to
the actual target’s Grappled rating. Greater restriction applies when combined with
Dazed, not their sum. Prone is binary. Hidden is universal, not observer-by-observer.

A mixed permanent/temporary bookkeeping rule is recorded in the full condition reference.
Do not let a new temporary effect become permanent merely because another is starred.

## Summons, exploration and recovery

**Summoned forms — approved October 16, 2026:** summons are shaped from energies
to resemble and act like their creatures, not actual physical creatures brought
into the scene. They cannot be healed and disappear at 0 HP, leaving no body.
Ordinary unsummoned creatures retain their own healing rules.

Summoned forms remain tangible: they occupy squares, block movement, take damage
and can be pushed or grappled normally unless their card says otherwise. Their
energy composition grants no automatic incorporeality or damage/control immunity.

Summons require commands; see the [summoning reference](summoning.md). Without a
command they do nothing, including following, lookout and alerts. Old orders grant
no continued activity; existing conditions and durations still resolve. No free independent
turns, inherent Reactions or summon chains. No count cap. Beyond 6 squares from the
controller they disappear, including forced movement of either participant.
Measure between the nearest occupied squares of controller and summon, using
ordinary grid distance; this applies to every footprint. Exactly 6 squares is
within the tether; beyond 6 causes immediate disappearance.

**Summoned healing:** the controller pays the healing
ability’s printed SP cost instead of the summon, once, before resolution. The
controller must have sufficient SP. Use the summon’s
printed attribute and outcomes. Ordinary unsummoned healers pay their own cost.

Ordinary travel has no routine roll and no exhaustion track. Group checks occur
outside combat only: each participant adds 1/2/3 to a declared target. State binary
or cumulative before rolling. Make crafting and treatment rolls individually.

Safe overnight rest restores HP and SP; first aid uses one recipient allowance between rests. Scars are descriptive; Grit is gained once at levels 1/3/7 and never refreshes. At 0 HP heroes enter Dying; further damage causes an immediate Fortitude death roll. Weak adds a failure, Strong adds a success and Standard changes neither tally. Three failures kill unless Grit or an ability intervenes. Three successes stabilize at 0 HP. See [recovery](recovery.md) for the complete procedure.

[Latest perception, timing and movement decisions](session-resolution.md) supersede
earlier timing notes. [Full conditions](conditions.md), [scars](wounds.md), and
[encounter calibration](encounters.md) complete the current working references.

records.title: Languages
records.markdown:
# Languages

A familiar greeting can open a door that gold cannot. An inscription can preserve
an enemy's warning long after the enemy is dust. Languages tell you whom your hero
can understand and which voices shaped their life. They do not determine ancestry,
allegiance or character.


## Choose your languages

Begin with **Common and one other ordinary language** learned in the community
that raised you. Common is the campaign's shared trade language; the DA may give
it a local name. Choose your other language with the DA from the list below or
the campaign's equivalent. Any ancestry may know any language. Culture suggests
where you learned it, rather than imposing a compulsory choice.

Record the language's actual name, not just “regional” or “community language.”
If Common was your only home language, choose another ordinary language learned
through neighbors, work or travel. This starting choice is separate from your
culture's discipline and ability pair and costs no DP.

Apply explicit extra grants afterward. **A Foot in Two Worlds** lets a Human choose
another ancestry, learn one language native to it and gain one trait from its trait
list, while keeping Human base HP and Speed. A signed language is an ordinary
language when the campaign uses it. Follow any explicit restriction on a grant.

Unless a grant says otherwise, knowing a language includes speaking, understanding,
and reading and writing its usual script, if it has one. A grant that specifically
says *spoken*, *understands* or *cannot speak* keeps that restriction. Record such
limits beside the language. Speaking a language does not require a separate skill
rating, and attributes grant no automatic extra languages.

## Ordinary languages

These are starting options, not a required history of the world. Their names
describe familiar traditions; anyone raised among their speakers may learn them.
Each row is one language unless it explicitly asks you to name a particular one.

| Language | Where you might learn or encounter it |
|---|---|
| Common | Markets, mixed settlements, roads and adventuring companies. |
| Regional language | Choose one named local language: a river kingdom, island community or frontier valley. Each is a separate choice. |
| Dwarven | Deep halls, quarry towns and craft communities; records of lineage, work and agreements. |
| Elven | Woodland settlements and long-lived artistic traditions; songs, histories and correspondence. |
| Halfling | Hearth communities, traveling families and river villages; stories and everyday business. |
| Goblin | Goblin communities and their neighbors; salvage yards, markets and warrens. |
| Orc | Orc communities and their neighbors; border settlements, expeditions and oral histories. |
| Giant | Giant communities and peoples who trade with them; landmarks, stone records and remembered journeys. |
| Kobold | Kobold communities and their neighbors; tunnel works, workshops and trading posts. |
| Harbor Cant | Multilingual ports and ship crews. A full local language, not universal knowledge of every sailor's slang. |
| Way Sign | A complete signed language shared by participating communities. Communication requires sight and usable signing gestures. |

## Uncommon and ancient languages

These languages are not included in an unrestricted *ordinary language* grant.
Choose one only when a grant explicitly allows it or the DA makes it an ordinary
option for the campaign before character creation. Their availability reflects
the setting, not a higher numerical bonus.

| Language | Where it becomes useful |
|---|---|
| Draconic | Speaking with dragons and their learned allies; reading draconic inscriptions. Kobold is a separate language. |
| Fey | Negotiating with fey courts and woodland powers; understanding their stories and spoken bargains. |
| Infernal | Speaking with fiends and interpreting their correspondence or contracts. Knowing it does not bind or summon anything. |
| Celestial | Conversations with celestial beings and some sacred traditions. It grants no divine authority. |
| Elemental | Speech used by elemental beings capable of language. It does not let you command fire, weather or an unintelligent elemental. |
| Elder Tongue | Choose one named lost or ancient scholarly language. Different vanished civilizations need not share it. |

A sacred text may be written in Common, Dwarven or any other language. “Sacred,”
“scholarly” and “courtly” describe use, not automatic additional languages.
Beasts' calls, a spirit's images and a construct's signal lights are forms of
communication, not languages you gain by choosing a row in these tables.

## Use languages at the table

When you share a language and can hear, see or read it as required, ordinary
communication needs no roll. State what you say or ask. A conversation can still
involve uncertainty about persuasion, deception or evidence; use the normal
attribute or the ability you declared. Knowing the words does not make the listener
agree, reveal secrets or recognize your authority.

A language barrier is not simply extra Banes on a roll. Without a shared means of
communication, you cannot deliver a precise argument merely by rolling well.
Pointing, drawing or demonstrating can convey something simple: “danger there,”
“follow me,” or an offered trade. Agree on what is actually understood. An interpreter,
a translation, or an applicable ability can make a more complicated exchange possible.
A card that explicitly requires a shared language still requires one; an interpreter
does not silently change its target requirement.

Reading a clear message in a language you can read needs no roll. Damaged text,
an unfamiliar technical subject or a cipher may present a separate problem.
Sharing an alphabet does not grant another language, and a cipher is not an extra
language choice. Ask the DA what evidence or expertise could make progress possible.

**Translate the Fragment** supplies a way to interpret unfamiliar written text.
Use its printed time, progress and outcomes. Completing a translation does not
teach you the whole language. A copied voice or disguise likewise supplies no
vocabulary or memories unless its ability explicitly says so.

## Learn another language

[Another Tongue](../cards/another-tongue.md) costs 1 DP and grants one additional
ordinary language, including its usual script if it has one. It requires no
discipline and may be purchased once, during level-0 creation or later. Record
the language you choose. This is a specific card grant, not a repeatable price
for buying every language or permission to learn a secret language.

## Keep learning grounded

Record new languages when an explicit trait, ability or agreed campaign grant
provides them. Time with a teacher, a community or useful texts explains that
learning; it does not create an unstated free advancement or a new universal DP
price. Agree on the route before spending time or DP. Translation and ordinary
practice remain useful even when they do not grant permanent fluency.

> **At the gate.** An elf raised in a dwarven mining town chooses Common and
> Dwarven. She reads the quarry's warning without a roll. Its damaged diagram
> still needs investigation. Her human companion chose Goblin for A Foot in Two
> Worlds and learned Goblin; he can question a salvager and read the written ledger.

records.title: Learning and using disciplines
records.markdown:
# Learning and using disciplines

A discipline offers four paths of practice. Spend 1 DP to begin studying it, then choose a path and learn its first ability. Within each path, learn the first ability, its two improvements and then its final ability, in that order. The four steps cost 1, 2, 2 and 3 DP. Each entry is learned once. Improvements remain active together and affect only the named ability. The final ability is separate unless it explicitly uses the earlier technique.

You may learn disciplines and their first three steps during level-0 or level-1 development. The final ability requires character level 3. I names the first ability. II and III mark its improvements. Learning one path never requires learning another path in that discipline. Every hero can make basic attacks, speak, climb, search and help someone. Discipline paths develop those everyday capabilities into practiced techniques.

When an improvement replaces a number, use the new total rather than adding both totals. For example, Driving Blow II pushes 2 squares instead of 1; Driving Blow III adds Dazed 1. On Strong, both the 2-square push and Dazed apply. There is no choice between them. Only explicit choices such as a destination or target remain.

## Common action rules

Damage and progress written as three numbers mean Weak / Standard / Strong. Roll 3d6 plus the stated attribute, applying normal Boons and Banes: Weak is 8 or less, Standard 9–14, Strong 15 or more. For attacks against your hero, you roll the printed defense. For exchanges between NPCs, a player or the DA rolls using the NPC procedure.

Every attack hits. Remove immune damage types, then apply weakness, matching resistance and other reductions. Keep the final minimum of 1 if any positive damage component survived immunity. Reducing a condition or forced movement to 0 is permitted: those are not damage. Attack damage is instant; conditions follow their normal timing and decay unless an ability states a duration. Stability and any explicit forced-movement defenses still apply.

An ability costs its printed action every time it is used. A Reaction needs its stated trigger and an available Reaction; no entry here grants additional Reactions. An improvement costs no separate action unless stated. Passive training works while its requirements hold. A time such as 10 minutes is the uninterrupted work required for each roll; it is not a combat Main Action. Normal condition restrictions and action conversions still apply.

Targets must be reachable as the ability describes. Movement requires an unoccupied legal destination and a feasible route; it stops at barriers. When forced movement meets a creature or barrier, use the collision rules in Playing the Game. Other movement uses the usual movement-reaction rules unless the entry explicitly avoids them. An ability with a choice of up to several targets can affect each target only once per use.

Gather the equipment your chosen technique uses. An entry that provides equipment describes what you receive. Ordinary recipes and ingredients retain their existing inventory and price rules. Smoke ingredients use one ordinary recipe ingredient batch per flask, with price and availability set before preparation; finished flasks have Bulk 1 each. Prepared products persist until used or spoiled. Craft covers ordinary construction and preparation; use the appropriate magical working to create enchanted items.

# Objectives and progress

Use an objective when success takes more than one useful contribution: repairing a gate, following a trail, translating a passage or convincing a reluctant listener. Ordinary actions remain available without a learned ability. Learned abilities change the time, progress, reach or effects of those actions.

## Set the objective before rolling

The Dungeon Architect states the concrete result, what evidence or resources are needed, and how much progress completes it. Use 3 progress for a modest task, 6 for a substantial task, 9 for a demanding task and 12 for an exceptional task. These are reference values; the DA chooses the objective level appropriate to the situation. Impossible tasks do not become possible through accumulated rolls.

The DA also states the work interval, deadline and known consequences. A printed ability supplies its own interval and progress results. An ordinary feasible contribution adds 1/2/3 progress with the attribute appropriate to the approach. Progress is shared only when contributions genuinely serve the same objective. Another person may Aid or make their own contribution during an interval, not both. Craft projects remain individual.

At the target, resolve the stated result. Extra progress does not spill into unrelated objectives. Weak still makes progress; it is not a failure to act. Natural retained 111 adds a complication, and 666 adds a benefit, as in the core resolution rules. No routine extra penalty is attached merely to a Weak result. The DA may track a separate deadline or danger established before the attempt.

## Social encounters

State the concession sought and who can grant it. The DA determines whether persuasion, evidence, deception, a bargain or pressure can work. Set one objective for listeners who share a motive; use separate objectives for listeners with different interests. State known boundaries and deal-breakers before the roll when the characters could recognize them.

An exchange is one meaningful statement or response, normally about a minute outside combat. In combat, an exchange costs a Main Action. Listeners must be able to perceive and understand the approach. A new roll needs a new relevant fact, offer, demonstration or changed circumstance. Repeating the same argument earns no progress. Different speakers cannot obtain extra rolls by repeating it.

Completing an attainable objective earns the agreed concession, not control over the listener. It cannot override a player's decisions, invent consent, erase an enemy's motives or force an impossible bargain. Changed circumstances may require a new objective; the DA explains why existing progress no longer answers the problem. Unsupported claims may be inapplicable, but a permitted Weak roll still advances the objective.

Example: a keeper needs assurance before opening a gate. The DA sets 6 progress to gain entry, requiring a credible reason and a guarantee against trouble. A Standard Make the Case II contributes 3. A companion presents a relevant letter and rolls Standard on an ordinary Reason contribution for 2. The first speaker adds a new offer and rolls Weak for 1: the gate opens under the agreed terms.

## Medicine and recovery

With suitable supplies, anyone can give first aid. Spend 10 minutes and roll Knowledge to restore 2/4/6 HP. Each recipient can receive one first-aid treatment between safe overnight rests. The recipient can use that attempt for ordinary first aid or a learned treatment such as Field Dressing. All healers share the same allowance.

Condition care treats specific conditions. Apply the treatment’s listed condition reductions and any HP recovery it provides.

A safe overnight rest takes 8 hours, including 6 hours of sleep and 2 quiet hours, and restores HP and SP once per 24 hours. Shelter alone does not guarantee safety. Track treatment through HP and the recipient’s first-aid allowance. Scars remain part of the hero’s story. Use the Stabilize Maneuver to help an adjacent Dying hero. The hero stays at 0 HP and clears both death roll tallies. Further damage at 0 causes an immediate death roll.

records.title: Magic and spellbooks
records.markdown:
# Magic and spellbooks

A spellbook gathers a related family of spells. Its colored rows show the sections you learn as your studies deepen; each page adds a spell to your repertoire.

## Learning your books

Begin studying a magical discipline for 1 DP, then choose a book. Learn its sections in order: I costs 1 DP and teaches pages 1–2; II costs 2 DP and teaches pages 3–4; III costs 2 DP and teaches pages 5–6. At character level 3, learn section IV for 3 DP: it teaches pages 7–8 and all three advanced pages, A1–A3. Record the named final section for any combined abilities that call for it.

The first page of every book costs 0 SP to cast. Keep every learned page available for use. Spellcraft offers three training paths and the Channeling book; its capacity paths add to your shared SP reserve.

## Casting a spell

Choose a learned spell and legal targets, and commit its stated action. Resolve any opportunity attack first. If you can continue, recheck your targets, pay the printed SP and resolve the spell. You need a free hand and a clear path to a target unless the spell describes a remote connection. Measure range in squares from your position. A point or destination must be visible when chosen unless the spell explicitly uses a known place, memory, object or person instead. Carry ordinary gear within your usual capacity when a spell transports you.

Use the spell's printed attribute for any roll. A block marked Automatic resolves its stated effect directly. Three values always mean Weak / Standard / Strong. Attacks use the familiar 3d6 resolution and the normal rules for immunity, resistance and minimum damage. Apply a condition at its listed rating unless the target is immune to that condition, then use its normal timing and decay. Apply healing after the recipient's Life resistance, restore at least 1 HP when HP is missing, and stop at maximum HP. Healing spends SP independently of the recipient's first-aid treatment.

For several targets, work out the relevant Boons and Banes for each, roll once using the combination least favorable to you, and apply the result to every target. A spell that says every creature includes allies. A spell that says choose or up to a number lets you select its recipients. Affect each creature once per casting, even if it occupies several squares in the area. A cone widens from your square to the stated width at its far edge; a line is one square wide. Count radius distance using normal grid distance.

Players make the rolls. When an NPC casts against heroes, each affected player rolls the appropriate defense: Fortitude against bodily alteration, poison or life drain; Agility against aimed rays, bursts and moving hazards; Reason against thought, emotion, divination or magical binding. A spell or creature profile may name a more specific defense. Read the caster's outcomes in reverse: a Weak defense receives its Strong effect, Standard receives Standard, and Strong receives Weak. For an NPC-only exchange use the ordinary DA resolution procedure. Resolve automatic environmental and willing effects as printed.

## Actions and Rituals

**Main Action** spells include attacks, substantial healing, battlefield control and summoning. Attack cantrips also use a Main Action. **Maneuver** spells handle brief, small effects, such as sending a message, lighting an object or moving a small item. The action printed in each spell is the procedure to use.

A **Reaction** spell names its trigger and when to respond. Spend your available Reaction when that event occurs. A defense bonus applies before the roll; a reduction or redirection applies at the timing stated in its block. The ordinary action conversions still apply to casting, including using a Main Action for a Maneuver spell.

A **Ritual** gives its required casting time alongside the label. Pay SP and supply any listed materials at the beginning, following a printed daily schedule or payment timing when given. Work continuously for the stated time or scheduled work period, keeping the required subjects and materials present. Finish the Ritual before receiving its effect. An interrupted Ritual must be started again with fresh costs. Ritual work is active activity rather than restorative rest. Materials described as consumed are used up by the attempt at the printed time, or at the beginning when no time is given.

## Duration and sustained magic

An instant spell resolves once. A fixed-duration spell lasts for its printed time. In combat, count 10 rounds for each minute. You may end your own ongoing spell with a Maneuver. When it changes ordinary material permanently, the resulting object or terrain follows ordinary rules afterward. A magical effect ending leaves its described consequences in place: healed HP stays restored and damage stays dealt.

For a spell marked **Sustained**, casting maintains it until the end of your next turn. Starting on the turn after you cast it, spend a Maneuver and 1 SP by the end of each turn to maintain it through the end of your following turn, within the printed maximum duration. Perform that upkeep once per turn. A Main Action may convert to the required Maneuver. The upkeep's listed movement or renewal is part of that same Maneuver. A separate attack or other activity that names a Main Action still uses it.

You may sustain one spell at a time. Beginning another sustained spell ends the previous one. Unconsciousness, death, or missing an upkeep ends sustain. If a block says a condition is renewed, raise that spell's remaining contribution to the named rating rather than adding another instance each round. Conditions decay normally after renewal ends.

Identical named ongoing benefits on one recipient use the strongest value and the latest expiry; repeated castings refresh rather than multiply the benefit. Each independent damaging zone follows its stated per-round limit. Resolve damage when entering or ending a turn in such a zone, as printed; forced movement can cause entry. A round begins with the first creature's turn and ends after the last creature's turn.

## Summons, forms and invitations

A spell that creates a summoned form uses its listed profile, one immediate Main command on arrival, continuing commands and the six-square tether from Summoned Companions. Commands maintain these forms for the printed duration; they use the command procedure rather than sustained-spell upkeep. Their HP tracks the form, and they disperse at 0 HP or when their controller becomes unconscious or dies. Healing they perform spends the controller's SP. Summoned forms receive activity through commands and return to energy when their duration ends.

The roster's ratings 1, 3 and 7 describe which profiles a calling can produce. The spell names its permitted category and maximum rating. Use the summoned profile rather than the DA creature's combat entry. Animal shapes worn by a hero instead keep that hero's HP, attributes and resources, using the spell's stated movement and natural attacks.

A Familiar bond or invitation to a named planar being concerns an independent creature. It keeps its own needs, choices and relationships. Negotiate its service through the ordinary social procedures. A resurrection restores the named person only with that person's agreement. Lifegiving, Mass Lifegiving and True Resurrection share one lifetime return per person; Grit is separate.

## Illusions and informed choices

An illusion creates the sights, sounds or sensations its block describes. Physical interaction reveals an insubstantial image. To study a plausible illusion by observation, a hero spends a Main Action and rolls Reason for 1/2/3 progress toward target 3. Once complete, the hero recognizes it. When an NPC examines a hero's illusion, the player rolls Guile and the observer gains 3/2/1 progress on the player's Weak/Standard/Strong result. Keep that observer's progress for that illusion. Sound alone reveals no physical barrier or support.

Mental and social spells state the information, progress, conditions or choices they provide. Use the social objective procedure for concessions, with the DA setting a feasible goal around the listener's motives. A hero's player supplies their character's private thoughts or chooses their response where the spell calls for one. A spell that offers a command or resistance effect gives that choice to the target's controller.

## Unraveling a spell

Cancellation is progress against a particular casting. Its target is **2 + the spell's printed SP cost**, unless the effect states its own remedy. Use the target of the affected spell rather than any extra SP spent transferring or sustaining it. Keep accumulated progress while that same casting remains active. Completing the objective ends that casting; incomplete progress expires when it ends. A Reaction that interrupts casting must reach its target during that trigger to prevent resolution. Its block states any partial effect.

Spellbook spells, including Rituals, may be unraveled when the cancellation entry can reach and identify the effect. Removing a lasting enchantment follows its explicit remedy or Unessence. A specific remedy such as Remove Curse may end an effect immediately when the effect says so. Ordinary material shaped by a completed spell remains an ordinary object afterward.

## Sharing Spell Points

Casting and upkeep costs are paid separately from any SP moved. Transfer existing points from a donor's current reserve into a recipient's missing SP; the amount moved is the smallest of the spell's limit, the donor's available points, and the recipient's remaining capacity. Subtract the exact amount received from the donor. A reserve of 0 transfers 0.

Choose two different personal reserves for a transfer. A summoned form, animated group or magical duplicate uses its controller's resource rules and provides no independent SP reserve. A willing donor chooses its contribution. For unwilling participants, use the printed roll and the ordinary player-facing defense procedure; transferred SP itself causes no HP damage. A redirected transfer resolves once to its final recipient.

A transmitted spell uses its own action category and costs as stated by the channeling block. Its original caster makes any casting roll and handles sustain; the releasing ally uses the named Reaction. Rituals retain their full ritual time and preparation, and are outside effects that explicitly transmit a Main Action spell.

Choose a spell from outside the Channeling book when you use Channel Spell or Lord Channels. Channeling one of the book's own spells would send the magic back as arcane feedback.

records.title: Harm and Recovery
records.markdown:
# Harm and Recovery

Your HP measures how much danger you can endure before you fall. Rest, treatment
and magic restore it. Grit is the courage that brings you back when ordinary
endurance fails. Scars remember what happened after the numbers recover.

## HP and growing endurance

At level 0, maximum HP is **10 + ancestry HP contribution + Fortitude + explicit
HP benefits**. At level 1, add your class HP contribution. At every level after
1, add your ancestry and class HP contributions again. Each contribution is 1,
2 or 3; record their sum as your HP gain per level. Fortitude and fixed benefits
are added once, not multiplied by level.

For level 1 or higher: **maximum HP = 10 + level × (ancestry + class HP
contributions) + Fortitude + explicit HP benefits**. On gaining a level, increase
current HP by the same amount as maximum HP; this does not end Dying or restore
HP to a character at 0. Such a character gains the maximum only until recovered.

Damage reduces current HP, to a minimum of 0. Healing restores the stated amount,
up to maximum HP. Apply Life resistance to magical healing and potions, with a
minimum of 1 actual healing when HP is missing. First aid and rest are not Life
magic and ignore Life resistance. Healing cannot restore the dead.

## Falling to 0 HP

A player character reduced from positive HP to 0 enters **Dying**, falls prone
and becomes unconscious. Start each Dying episode with zero failure marks and
zero success marks. Ordinary NPCs and creatures normally die at 0. Summoned
forms disappear.

At the start of each Dying turn, make a **Fortitude death roll** using 3d6 and
the usual Boons and Banes. Use only the result band for this roll, even on
retained triples.

| Death-roll result | Effect |
|---|---|
| Weak | Add 1 failure mark. |
| Standard | Keep both tallies as they are. |
| Strong | Add 1 success mark. |

Track failures and successes separately throughout the episode. On your **third
success**, stabilize at 0 HP and clear both tallies. On your **third failure**,
you die unless you spend Grit or an ability intervenes at its stated trigger.

**Last Words.** If your hero dies, you can describe their final words, gesture
or silence as part of that moment.

### Further damage

Taking damage while already at 0 HP causes **one immediate death roll** per event. An event that deals 0 damage leaves the tallies alone.
Apply the death roll's result once for the whole event. Later events such as
Bleeding or Burning each trigger their own roll. Damage while stabilized
first returns you to Dying, then causes this immediate roll. The event that first
reduces positive HP to 0 does not also cause an immediate death roll.

Resolve the damage and immediate death roll before moving on to the next event.
If healing or Grit restores positive HP, later damage reduces that HP normally.
Keep turn timing until Dying and immediate hazards have been resolved; ending a
battle does not skip death rolls.

## Stabilization and recovery at 0

Anyone can use the **Stabilize Maneuver** on an adjacent Dying hero, without a roll
or supplies. Clear both tallies and end Dying, leaving them at **0 HP**. They
regain consciousness from HP loss, but remain prone and cannot take Main Actions,
Maneuvers, Reactions or voluntary movement until they regain HP. Apply the same three defense Banes as Unconscious while at 0. They can speak,
perceive their surroundings and accept help. Companions can carry them. Another
source of unconsciousness or incapacity still follows its own remedy.

A stabilized hero makes no turn-start death rolls. Further damage restarts Dying.
Healing above 0 ends Dying, clears both tallies and ends HP-caused unconsciousness; it
does not automatically stand the hero up or remove other conditions. Healing may
target a Dying or stabilized hero without requiring consent or a Reaction.

## Grit: three chances across a career

Gain **1 Grit at level 1**, **1 more at level 3**, and **1 more at level 7**. Record
each grant and each expenditure. Grit never refreshes through rest, treatment,
magic or a new session. Unspent points carry forward; spending one removes it
permanently. These milestones are the only Grit grants.

Spend one Grit when you fall to 0, at the start of a Dying turn, immediately after
a death roll adds a failure mark (including the third failure), or while
stabilized at 0. This costs no action or Reaction. Set current HP to **half maximum HP, rounded up**, clear both tallies, and end Dying and HP-caused
unconsciousness. Other conditions remain. If an ability makes HP unavailable
for recovery, apply that limit to Grit as well.

> **Example — a third failure.** You have 17 maximum HP, two failures and one
> success. You roll Weak. Before death becomes final, you spend your last Grit.
> Set HP to 9 and clear both tallies.

## Scars tell the story

Surviving an incident in which you reached 0 HP leaves a permanent descriptive
scar. Choose it with the DA once the danger has passed: a pale seam, singed hair,
a shaking hand when thunder sounds, or a remembered voice. One incident can include
several falls and rescues; it leaves one scar, rather than a new entry for every
hit at 0. A later incident can add another.

A scar changes no attribute, HP, movement, Boons, Banes or future death rolls. It
cannot require a treatment track or remove a body part. Its emotional meaning
belongs to the player. Treatment and healing restore capability without erasing
history. See [Scars and Survival](wounds.md) for prompts.

## Safe overnight rest

After **eight hours in a place the DA judges safe**, with food, water and adequate
shelter, restore full HP and SP and renew your first-aid allowance. Include at least
six hours of sleep or equivalent rest; the other two can include quiet activity
or a watch. Oath-Bound use the same rest period, with stillness in place of sleep.
You can gain these benefits only once in 24 hours.

A fight, strenuous work or forced travel interrupts the rest; complete a new
uninterrupted period afterward. Brief waking, conversation and routine watch do
not. The DA explains what makes a campsite unsafe before the group commits to it.
A stabilized hero can recover this way; a Dying hero must first be stabilized.

During a shorter pause, you can treat injuries or use a learned recovery
ability when you meet its requirements. Grit stays spent, scars remain and
lasting conditions follow their own remedies.

## First aid and treatment

Stabilization is the immediate rescue. **First Aid** is slower care that anyone can
provide: spend **ten uninterrupted minutes**, use one supply of clean dressings
and medicine, and make a **Knowledge roll** for yourself or one willing, Dying or
stabilized living creature within reach. Restore **2/4/6 HP** on Weak/Standard/Strong.
Resolve the supply's inventory die after use. A Dying patient continues making death rolls during treatment. Stabilize
them first when possible.

Each recipient can receive **one treatment attempt between safe overnight rests**,
shared by all healers. Use ordinary first aid or a learned treatment such as
Field Dressing for that attempt. Mark the allowance and use the supply when you
begin, then restore HP when you finish. You can stabilize someone or reduce
a condition separately. Treat starred conditions with the remedy listed by
their source.

## Magical healing and spell points

Your SP reserve is separate from HP. Add **1 SP from ancestry, 1 from culture,
1 from background and 3 from class**: 3 maximum SP at level 0, 6 at level 1, before
explicit improvements. These starting contributions are added once. From level 2 onward, gain **2 maximum SP each level**. At level 1 and later, maximum SP is **6 + 2 × (level − 1) + learned capacity and other explicit benefits**. Track current SP separately from this maximum. A safe overnight rest fills
the reserve. Learned recovery follows its own timing.

Healing magic spends the caster's printed **SP cost before resolution**, whether
used in battle or during quiet time. Keep a free hand and follow the spell's range. Cast as often as you have the
SP and time. The recipient keeps their first-aid allowance for treatment.
For a potion, use its printed healing and check its inventory die.

A summoned healer's controller pays the SP cost. Summoned energy forms cannot
receive healing and disappear at 0 HP. No ability may turn HP healing into SP
recovery unless it explicitly supplies that conversion.

## Conditions keep their own rules

At turn end, resolve a temporary numbered condition, then reduce its rating by 1.
A starred contribution has no automatic decay; use its source's remedy. Keep
starred and temporary contributions separate. Scars never apply conditions.

Spend a Main Action and use a plausible method to reduce Bleeding, Burning or
Freezing on yourself or an adjacent creature by 1, without a roll. This does not
heal HP or consume first aid. Other conditions use their own removal procedures.
A curse can persist through an overnight rest even though the hero's HP returns.

A non-player healer without a separately printed SP reserve has 6 SP. Summoned forms use their controller’s reserve instead.

records.title: Perception, interruption and movement
records.markdown:
# Perception, interruption and movement

## Player rolls — agreed

When a player looks for something, the DA calls for **Reason**, with Boons/Banes
for circumstances. When someone might perceive a hidden player character, that
player rolls **Agility** to remain Hidden. Do not add an opposed observer roll.
Ordinary obvious information requires no roll. Hidden remains universal; actual
concealment and a plausible approach matter.

**Procedure:** active searching or attempting to hide during
combat costs a Main Action unless a card states otherwise. A hidden creature that
attacks or openly reveals itself loses Hidden. No roll conceals someone in plain
view with no plausible concealment. Establish progress and consequences before an unscripted roll. A Weak search
might narrow the location; a Weak hiding attempt might reach cover while leaving
evidence. These examples do not override the scene or a card’s printed outcomes.

## Opportunities — agreed

Starting a provoking action triggers the opportunity attack **before** that action
resolves. A hero uses Basic Melee with a held melee weapon or Basic Unarmed with a
free hand. A DA creature uses its bestiary Basic Melee. Use the usual single-roll
procedure for that attack. Then the original action continues if its actor is still
capable; otherwise it stops. Damage alone does not automatically cancel the action.
Forced movement never provokes.

Leaving melee reach voluntarily, including by crawling, can provoke. Casting a
spell beside an enemy, standing, stowing and retrieving items can also provoke.
Drawing as part of an attack stays part of that attack. **Timing:** commit
the action when declared; check targets and capability again after interruption;
pay an additional printed SP/HP/item cost only when continuing into its resolution.
If interrupted permanently, the committed action is spent but an unspent potion or
SP or HP cost is not consumed.

## Player-controlled creatures — agreed

Creature cards must print attack and defense attributes. The controlling player
rolls those printed creature attributes, not their character’s attribute. When an
NPC attacks a player-controlled summon, its controller rolls the summon’s defense.
When the summon attacks, its controller makes the attack roll. Use the ordinary
single-roll attack/defense outcome mapping. A player-controlled attacker does not
also cause a second player defense roll.

A summon disappears when its controller becomes unconscious or dies. An
uncommanded summon does nothing; existing effects and conditions still resolve.

## NPC-only resolution — approved October 16, 2026

Either a player or the DA assuming the player role can roll for NPC-only actions.
For an NPC attacking another NPC, roll the defending NPC’s printed attribute
named by the attack, with the applicable modifiers. Read the attacking creature’s
Weak / Standard / Strong defense outcomes. Make only one roll, not an opposed pair.

For consequential NPC healing or another task, the same choice of roller uses
the acting NPC’s printed attribute and outcomes. This does not transfer control
of the NPC to the person handling the dice. Existing player-character and
player-controlled creature procedures remain unchanged.

For example, when a bandit attacks an allied guard with an Agility-defense attack,
a player or the DA rolls the guard’s Agility defense and reads the bandit’s card.
Off-screen events may be resolved by DA judgment without rolling through unseen
combat.

## Stability and ordinary movement

**Stability — approved:** all characters and creatures start at 0; only an explicit
trait, ability or item raises it, maximum 3, highest source only. It consumes forced
movement once for the initial target and once for each new creature struck in a
collision chain. Stop when movement is exhausted; never charge a creature twice.
It does not resist Prone, grapples or conditions. See [Stability](stability.md) for
a worked example. **Collision timing approved October 16, 2026:** resolve contact
collision damage from movement remaining on arrival, then deduct the new member’s
Stability before further travel. Applicable resistance still reduces damage.

**Agreed:** falling deals **3 HP per 2 squares fallen**. **Rounding and damage:**
use 3 × floor(distance / 2), physical damage with ordinary physical resistance;
falls under 2 squares deal no automatic damage. Exceptional landing surfaces and circumstances are DA rulings.

**Agreed:** climbing and swimming use difficult-terrain movement cost, normally
2 per square, unless an ability changes it. Impossible surfaces and impassable
currents do not become traversable merely by spending movement. Roll only when
uncertainty has consequences. Cards can improve the ordinary activity.

**Jumping — approved:** broad jump up to max(1, 2 + Agility) squares; high jump up to
max(0, 1 + floor(Agility / 2)) squares. Each square traveled spends movement; a
broad jump needs 2 squares of approach, otherwise halve its maximum, rounded down
(minimum 1). A high jump needs no approach. Land in a legal supported free square;
no extra movement or passage through barriers. Negative Agility can mean no full
square of high-jump clearance, not inability to hop over a small obstacle. Obstacles
below a square and risky landings are adjudicated normally. No roll for a clear,
safe jump within these limits; risky execution can call for Agility. These values are approved; specialist movement cards retain their explicit exceptions.

## Consequence vocabulary

A **consequence** is what is at stake: harm, lost time, exposure, lost supplies,
a worsened position or an opportunity that closes. A **complication** introduces
an additional problem while retaining whatever progress the roll achieved. A
**benefit** adds a useful advantage. State the stakes before rolling. Weak is
progress, not automatic success; Strong is success with the printed result. Natural
111 adds a complication to Weak; 666 adds a benefit to Strong.

Use **1 Bane** for a meaningful obstacle, **2** for a severe obstacle, **3** for an
exceptional obstacle that remains possible. Use Boons symmetrically for real help
or advantageous circumstances. These are DA guidance bands, not target numbers.
Cancel Boons/Banes and apply the existing net cap of 3. Do not roll impossible
attempts or apply the same obstacle twice under different names. Group progress
and binary/cumulative task targets keep their existing rules.

## Magic and healing

Use the [spellbook rules](magic.md) for casting, Rituals, sustain and cancellation.
A character can unravel a casting through an ability that names a cancellation
procedure. Its usual target is 2 + the affected spell's printed SP cost.

Healing aimed at a creature whose profile says healing harms it becomes a Life
attack. Keep the spell's action, range, free hand and SP cost. Resolve its
printed healing values as Life damage, using the spell's attribute or the
target's applicable player defense. Recovery benefits apply only to healing.

records.title: Stability
records.markdown:
# Stability

**Approved by Bruce, October 13, 2026.** Every character and creature starts with
Stability 0. An ancestry trait, ability, equipment card or printed creature trait
must explicitly grant a higher value. Stability is not calculated from attributes,
ancestry size, armor, HP or level. Use the highest applicable grant, never their
sum, to a maximum of **3**.

Stability consumes the movement of a push, pull, slide or throw, minimum 0. Apply the
initial target’s Stability once before it moves. When the moving group strikes a
new creature, that creature’s Stability consumes remaining movement once as it
joins the chain, after contact collision damage resolves. If none remains, the group
stops. Never charge the same creature twice during one forced movement, even if
several occupied squares collide.

Stability does not resist Prone, grappling, conditions or damage. It does not
reduce voluntary movement or a thrown projectile’s range. A printed push of 1 can
therefore move a Stability-0 target but not a Stability-1 target; its other effects
still resolve. A stopped push does not erase the attack’s damage or conditions.

**Example:** a push of 5 strikes a creature with Stability 1, leaving 4. It moves
one normal square, leaving 3, then strikes a creature with Stability 2. That new
contact deals 3 collision damage to both participants, subject to applicable
resistance. The newly struck creature’s Stability then consumes 2, leaving 1 for
the moving group: enough to move one more normal square before stopping.

Use the existing terrain and collision rules. Spending Stability does not itself
create damage. **Collision timing — approved October 16, 2026:** resolve contact
collision damage using the movement remaining on arrival, then deduct the new member’s Stability
before further travel. This preserves an impact even when the new member stops
the chain. Stability resists displacement; applicable resistance reduces damage.

## Crowded moving groups — approved October 16, 2026

Move the group together along the forced-movement path. Its members must finish in
separate legal spaces. If the group cannot fit, stop at the last position where
everyone can fit. The DA determines the exact arrangement.

Placement cannot send a creature through a wall or grant extra forward movement.
Resolve any bounce after placing the group. Follow the [collision rules](foundations.md#movement)
for impacts and a blocked bounce. Placement does not erase an impact.

records.title: Summoning: choice and commands
records.markdown:
# Summoning: choice and commands

## Choose a creature, not another spell

Each summoning spell specifies its category, maximum eligible roster rating, placement and duration. Choose a listed profile in that category at or below the printed rating. The six families are Animal, Fey, Spirit, Elemental, Undead and Construct. Ratings 1, 3 and 7 identify the available profiles; learned spellbook pages determine which callings you can cast. A spell that names a particular profile uses that profile directly.

A category is an explicit bestiary tag. A ghost is not automatically selectable
under both Spirit and Undead; its entry must say so. These are summoned forms, not
permission to seize an existing creature or extract permanent equipment.

## Summoned energy forms — approved October 16, 2026

A summon is shaped from energies to resemble and act like the chosen creature;
it is not an actual physical creature brought into the scene. It cannot be healed.
Its HP tracks how much damage the form can sustain. At 0 HP it disappears rather
than leaving a body. The existing duration, tether and controller-disappearance
rules still apply.

**Tangibility — approved October 16, 2026:** summoned forms occupy squares and
block movement normally. They can take damage and be pushed or grappled normally
unless their card explicitly says otherwise. Being made from energy does not
automatically make a summon incorporeal or grant damage or control immunities.

This restriction concerns receiving healing. A summon with a printed healing
ability can still heal an eligible other creature, with its controller paying the
printed cost as described below. Ordinary unsummoned creatures keep their own
healing rules. A printed harmful Life effect is damage, not healing.

## Pay for activity

Summoned creatures require your constant interaction and concentration to maintain
their presence in reality. At the end of your turn, each of your summons that
received no command during that turn disappears. The immediate command granted
when you summon a creature counts as its command for that turn.

**Agreed:** an uncommanded summon does nothing. It does not follow, keep watch,
alert its controller, continue attacking, search, help or perform a standing order.
It takes no independent Reaction, including an opportunity attack. A prior order
never pays for another turn. Outside combat the same rule prevents unattended
work, scouting or guard duty; the controller must actively spend the required time
and actions directing it.

- Controller spends **Main Action**: one summon receives **Main Action + Maneuver**.
- Controller spends **Maneuver**: one summon receives **Maneuver + movement**.
- A summon receives at most one command on the controller’s turn. The controller
  may spend these two actions on different summons.
- Normal conversions apply: Main → Maneuver → movement. There is no separate free
  movement grant in the Main-command package. For example, convert its Maneuver
  to movement to approach, then spend Main on an attack.
- A newly summoned creature receives the summoning spell’s immediate free Main
  command. That is its command for this turn; it cannot also receive a paid one.
- Resolve the granted activity on the controller’s turn. It cannot be banked for
  an enemy turn. No summon chains and no independent summon turns.

Commanding has no roll. Any permitted attack or task uses the summon profile’s
printed procedure. A command is not automatic success or a way to invent a skill.

## Healing through a summon

When a summoned creature uses a healing ability, its controller pays the ability’s
printed SP cost instead of the summon. Pay once, before resolving the ability,
from the controller’s SP reserve. The controller must have enough SP or the
ability cannot be used. The summon still uses its own printed attribute and healing
outcomes; its command and action requirements are unchanged.

For example, the Moon Hart’s Battle Mending costs its controller 3 SP, then the
player rolls the hart’s Reason for 5/10/15 healing. The hart does not also pay 3 SP.
An ordinary unsummoned healer continues to pay its own cost.

## Orders in ordinary language

These examples describe intent, not a new menu of abilities granted to every creature.

| Order | Execution within the paid package |
|---|---|
| Attack that creature | Use a permitted attack. A Main command can convert its Maneuver to movement to approach first. |
| Defend that spot | A Maneuver command supplies movement and Defend, if the profile permits Defend. It does not grant free attacks at intruders. |
| Move there / follow me | Use only the granted movement, with legal routes and endpoints. Following stops when that movement ends. |
| Move and hide | Move to real concealment, then use the profile’s printed hiding action if the remaining budget permits it. No automatic Hidden. |
| Move and keep watch | Move, then use its printed observation action if affordable. It can report what it notices during that commanded activity; no continuing lookout afterward. |
| Help them | Use Aid or a printed support ability, if permitted and affordable. |
| Fetch or handle this | Use permitted movement and interaction; anatomy, reach, carried Bulk and action costs still apply. |
| Track this | Use the profile’s tracking procedure and available senses. The command does not grant tracking expertise. |

If a creature lacks the required capability or the package lacks the necessary
actions, it cannot complete that order. A longer task needs continued commands
and the printed activity time; one spoken instruction never buys hours of labor.

## What still happens without a command

Until it disappears at the end of your turn, the creature remains present and can
be damaged or forcibly moved. Existing
conditions, durations, tether checks and already-resolved effects continue normally.
These are consequences, not permission for new activity. A previous Defend benefit
lasts only to its printed expiry; it does not renew itself.

## Six-square tether — approved October 16, 2026

Measure ordinary grid distance between the nearest occupied squares of the
controller and summon. Diagonals count normally as one square. The summon remains
present at a distance of 6 squares; if the nearest distance exceeds 6, it immediately
disappears. Voluntary or forced movement of either participant can break the tether.

For example, a large summon remains present with its nearest square 6 squares away
and its farthest square 7 away. If its nearest square becomes 7 squares away, it
disappears. Neither creature’s center nor farthest occupied square sets the distance.

The summon profile must anchor any “your turn” duration or condition tick to the
controller’s turn. Passive defenses such as resistance remain applicable. Do not
import automatic attacks, active auras or triggered abilities from a monster entry
without an explicit summon-profile procedure consistent with command-only activity.

## Bestiary selection

The [summon selection](../bestiary/summon-choices.md) provides 73 entries,
covering all six categories at tiers 1, 3 and 7. Each prints HP, all six attributes,
attack and target-defense attributes, movement, footprint, senses, resistance,
the no-healing rule, command options and restrictions. Category or CV alone never authorizes a creature.

The [creature procedure](../bestiary/procedure.md) and summon selection document
the permitted command activities. Use the approved tether measurement above and
the [moving-group placement rules](stability.md) where relevant. Use the entry itself, not a monster’s narrative tactics as a standing order. No activity, alerts or independent Reactions without the permitted command.

**Latest agreement:** summons disappear when their controller becomes unconscious
or dies. Players roll their creatures’ printed attack and defense attributes;
see [session resolution](session-resolution.md).

records.title: Vision and perception
records.markdown:
# Vision and perception

Light and perception determine what a hero can observe and target. An ability grants the sense, rating or range it names; use the shared definitions here to resolve it.

## Light and sight

In complete darkness, no one can see.

In low light, the Dungeon Architect assigns 1 to 3 Banes according to the level of darkness. Apply these Banes to observation attempts and actions that require vision.

| Illumination | Sight-related Banes |
|---|---:|
| Clear light | 0 |
| Dim light | 1 |
| Very dim light | 2 |
| Barely perceptible light | 3 |

The table gives guidance for describing a lighting penalty. Judge the light reaching the subject of the attempt and apply that penalty once to the roll. Other sources of Boons and Banes use the ordinary resolution rules.

## Low-Light Vision

Low-Light Vision has a rating. Ignore that many Banes imposed by low light, to a minimum of zero low-light Banes. Remove the ignored lighting Banes before combining the roll’s remaining Boons and Banes.

For example, in light imposing 3 Banes, Low-Light Vision 1 leaves 2 low-light Banes. Low-Light Vision 2 leaves 1. In complete darkness, no one can see.

## Seismic Vision

While touching a continuous solid surface, Seismic Vision lets you pinpoint moving creatures and objects touching that surface within the sense’s printed range. It works in complete darkness.

You may use this perception to target a creature or object it locates. Use the attack’s or ability’s ordinary range and require a clear path to the target.

For example, a Deep Dwarf with The Stone Tells You can pinpoint a creature moving across the same connected stone floor within 6 squares, even after the lantern goes out. They can target that creature with an ability whose range and clear path reach it.

## Other forms of perception

Sonar, seismic, thermal and spiritual perception are distinct forms of perception. A named sense uses its own means of gathering information. Its rules state what it perceives and how that information supports observation and targeting; its granting ability supplies any printed range.

records.title: Scars and Survival
