records.markdown:
# Scars and Survival

Every survived incident that brought a hero to 0 HP leaves a descriptive scar.
Choose it with the player after danger passes. Use these prompts to describe
what the hero remembers or carries with them. A scar never adds a mechanical penalty or benefit.

| What happened | A possible lasting reminder |
|---|---|
| Steel or claws | A pale line across the shoulder; a nick through an eyebrow |
| Fire or lightning | A silver streak of hair; branching marks on the arm |
| Cold | White fingertips; a patch of frost-pale skin |
| Crushing force | A seam along the jaw; a story about the shield that broke |
| Mental magic | A recurring dream; a phrase you remember when frightened |
| Radiant magic | A bright fleck in the iris; a sun-shaped mark |
| Life-draining magic | A white lock of hair; a shadow beneath the old injury |
| A desperate rescue | A companion's name tattooed beside the mark |

The player decides how a remembered event affects their hero's personality. Do not
impose trauma, disability or involuntary behavior as the price of surviving.
A chosen scar cannot justify an automatic Bane, lost action or movement penalty.

Record the scar, the incident and who helped you survive. No severity or treatment
track is needed. A later adventure may give the mark new meaning. The
[recovery rules](recovery.md) govern HP, stabilization, death rolls and Grit.

records.title: Develop a character
records.markdown:
# Develop a character

## Level 0: the life before adventure

Assign Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge and Reason from −2 through +2, totaling +3. Attributes stay fixed as you gain levels. Choose an ancestry and two of its five traits, then choose culture and background independently.

Choose one complete learning option from your culture and one from your background. Begin studying the discipline listed in each option and learn the accompanying ability or spellbook section. For each discipline or entry you already know, add 1 DP to this stage’s pool.

Receive 10 + Knowledge + Reason + Guile DP, including negative adjustments, plus duplicate compensation and explicit ancestry benefits. Spend these points to begin studying disciplines and learn their entries. Beginning a discipline costs 1 DP. Follow each path in order: its first three steps cost 1, 2 and 2 DP. The fourth step costs 3 DP and requires level 3. These steps are available at level 0 unless a higher level is printed. Close the stage; unused DP expires.

## Level 1: choose a class

Meet the class's two attribute minimums (normally 0 in each); Odd has none. Choose two distinct disciplines from its starting list. These disciplines establish your class training; develop their paths through further learning. Each duplicate gives 1 level-1 DP. Choose one level-1 class signature; no discipline requirement applies to that signature.

Receive a fresh 10 + Knowledge + Reason + Guile DP, plus this stage's duplicate compensation and explicit ancestry benefits. Study disciplines and learn entries at the same costs as at level 0. Meet each entry’s requirements before learning it. Spend the points for this stage before finishing level 1.

## Learning and spellbooks

Each nonmagical path teaches an ability I, then II and III improve that same ability. Those effects add together unless a new total replaces an earlier total. The final level-3 entry teaches a distinct ability. Every hero can make basic melee and ranged attacks. Arms and Marksmanship develop those fighting skills further.

A magical discipline opens four spellbooks. Each book's first section teaches pages 1–2, the second pages 3–4, the third pages 5–6, and the level-3 endpoint pages 7–8 plus all three pages of its advanced book. Learn sections for 1/2/2/3 DP. Once learned, page 1 costs 0 SP to cast. Spellcraft instead provides Soul Capacity, Mind Capacity, Recovery and the Channeling spellbook. Capacity increases add to one shared SP pool.

At level 7, learn a combined ability after learning all the final abilities or named spellbook sections it lists. Spend 3 DP for two disciplines, 4 DP for three, or 5 DP for four. Some combinations bring magical and nonmagical disciplines together.

The six independent 1-DP talents remain available once each: Another Tongue, Message by Heart, Catch That!, A Party Piece, Quick Exit and Look Over Here! Class signatures are gained at their milestones, not bought as additional independent abilities.

## Equipment and starting numbers

Gather the equipment your chosen techniques use; an entry that provides an item says so. A plain worn outfit is free. Buy weapons, armor, tools, food and other supplies from your starting coins: 40 + ancestry + culture + background + class contributions. Compatible abilities may share one weapon. Use your recipes to make items from the ingredients you gather.

At level 1 and later, maximum HP is 10 + level × (ancestry contribution + class contribution) + Fortitude + fixed benefits. At level 0, use 10 + ancestry contribution + Fortitude + fixed benefits. Each later level adds ancestry + class contributions; fixed benefits and Fortitude are not added again.

Capacity is 10 + 3 × Brawn. Every Bulk above capacity reduces Speed by 1. Speed is ancestry base + Agility − encumbrance, minimum 0. Stability starts at 0; use the highest explicit source, maximum 3. Matching resistance uses the highest value, maximum 3. Damage immunity removes the named damage type before resistance.

Ancestry, culture and background each contribute 1 maximum SP at level 0. Class adds 3 at level 1, giving 6 before explicit benefits. From level 2 onward, gain **2 maximum SP each level**. At level 1 and later, maximum SP is **6 + 2 × (level − 1) + learned capacity and other explicit benefits**. These gains enlarge the reserve; they do not restore spent SP. Safe overnight rest restores the full reserve. Learn spells by studying the sections of your spellbooks. Record current and maximum HP and SP separately, and mark first aid available. Start with no death roll marks or scars.

Gain 1 Grit at level 1, 1 at level 3 and 1 at level 7. Each point can be used once and is gone permanently; rest never restores it. Using Grit returns you to half maximum HP, rounded up. See [recovery](rules/recovery.md) for dying, scars, treatment and safe overnight rest.

## Advancement

The DA awards milestone levels. From level 2 onward, gain 8 + the new level in DP. Save these points or spend them when the DA judges you are somewhere safe. Add your ancestry and class contributions to maximum HP. If you have positive HP, add the same amount to current HP. At 0 HP, increase only your maximum.

At level 3, final branch abilities become available; gain 1 Grit and choose one level-3 class signature. At level 7, combined abilities become available; gain 1 Grit and choose one level-7 class signature. At other levels, gain the DP, HP and SP listed below.

| New level | DP | Other milestone |
|---|---:|---|
| 2 | 10 | HP and +2 SP growth |
| 3 | 11 | HP and +2 SP growth; final path entries; one signature; 1 Grit |
| 4 | 12 | HP and +2 SP growth |
| 5 | 13 | HP and +2 SP growth |
| 6 | 14 | HP and +2 SP growth |
| 7 | 15 | HP and +2 SP growth; combined abilities; one signature; 1 Grit |
| 8 | 16 | HP and +2 SP growth |
| 9 | 17 | HP and +2 SP growth |
| 10 | 18 | HP and +2 SP growth |

Record what you learned, including spellbook pages, and how much DP remains. You can use any learned entry when you meet its requirements.

records.title: Playing the Game
records.markdown:
# Playing the Game

A drawn blade changes the conversation. A broken bridge changes the journey. The
rules help you decide what those changes mean when timing, danger and the choices
of several characters meet.

Begin with what your hero is doing. You can use a learned ability, take a universal
action, or describe something the situation makes possible. The DA establishes the
circumstances and calls for a roll only when uncertainty has consequences.

## Resolve an action

When you use an ability, declare it **before rolling**. Read its requirements, choose
its targets and any printed options, and check range and equipment. Spend the action
and any required cost. Roll its attribute if instructed, then apply the complete
Weak, Standard or Strong outcome. Finally, record conditions and continuing effects.

An outcome is complete: do not add the Weak damage to the Standard damage. If a
Strong outcome includes an earlier benefit, it says so. Instant damage happens once;
a condition applied by that damage follows the condition's own timing.

A no-roll ability still costs its printed action. A treatment that takes an hour
cannot be completed in one combat turn merely because it is indexed as a Main Action.

## Boons, Banes and results

Roll three dice, plus one die for each net Boon or Bane, to a maximum of six dice.
With Boons, retain the best three; with Banes, retain the worst three. Add the
printed attribute once. Weak is 8 or less, Standard 9–14, and Strong 15 or more.

| Circumstance | Usual adjustment |
|---|---|
| Meaningful help or obstacle | 1 Boon or Bane |
| Substantial help or a severe obstacle | 2 Boons or Banes |
| Exceptional advantage or difficulty, still possible | 3 Boons or Banes |

These are guides for the DA. They do not turn an impossible attempt into a possible
one. Do not count the same obstacle twice under different names. Boons and Banes
from distinct valid sources stack, cancel, and then use the three-die net limit.

> **Example — keeping the best three.** An attack has 3 Boons and 1 Bane, leaving
> 2 Boons. Roll five dice. On 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, retain 4, 5, 6 for 15. Brawn +1 makes
> 16, a Strong result. If two Banes remained instead, retain 1, 2, 4 for 7; Brawn +1
> would give 8, a Weak result. Neither roll changes the attack's printed damage.

Read retained natural 111 as Weak with an additional complication and 666 as Strong
with an additional benefit. The result still makes its printed progress. The DA
fits a benefit or complication to the scene; it does not silently double damage or
grant another action. Death rolls use only the result band.

## Taking turns

A round lasts **6 seconds**, so 10 rounds make 1 minute. Each character takes
one turn during that time.

At the start of combat, the DA decides whether either side has pulled off an
ambush. If so, the ambushing side starts without an initiative roll. Otherwise,
one player rolls unmodified 3d6. On 12 or more, the players start. On 11 or less,
the opposition starts. The starting side opens **every round of this combat**.

An ambush comes from the setup, such as catching opponents unaware from cover.
Declaring an attack first leaves the usual initiative procedure in place. Both
sides take their usual turns in the first round. Use the ordinary rules for
concealment, cover and positioning.

The starting side chooses one of its characters to act. Then the other side chooses
one. Alternate until everyone has taken a turn. If one side has no characters left
to act, the other finishes its remaining turns. Each side chooses its order as it goes.

On your turn, you have one **Main Action**, one **Maneuver**, and movement up to your
**Speed**. You also have one **Reaction**, available for its stated trigger. Refresh
that turn's budget at the start of your turn. A defense roll does not itself spend
a Reaction. Choose your retained categories at turn start if Dazed or Grappled.

You can split movement around your actions. You can convert your Main Action into
a Maneuver and a Maneuver into another movement allowance. Conversion goes only
in that direction. Converting your Main and original Maneuver into movement gives
three total movement allowances: a full sprint.

> **Example — reaching an ally.** Speed 6 lets Mara move 6 squares. She converts her
> Maneuver into movement for 6 more, then uses her Main Action to heal a companion.
> She has not gained a second Main Action, and any difficult terrain costs still apply.

A Reaction resolves when its trigger says it does, including on someone else's turn.
Once spent, it is unavailable until refreshed. A free attack granted by an ability
spends no action and may occur more than once in a turn, but **free attacks never
trigger additional free attacks**. Read the granting effect to see which attack it allows.

## Attacking and defending

Players roll. When your hero attacks, roll the attack's printed attribute and read
its attacker outcomes. This is true even if the target is another player character;
the receiving player does not also roll a defense.

When a DA-controlled creature attacks you, roll the defense attribute specified by
that attack. It might be Agility to evade a blow, Fortitude to withstand a bodily
assault, or another attribute named by the attack. Apply the result from its
**Weak defense / Standard defense / Strong defense** columns. Weak defense is the
most dangerous outcome; Strong defense is the least dangerous.

| Player's defense | Equivalent attacker outcome |
|---|---|
| Weak | Strong attack |
| Standard | Standard attack |
| Strong | Weak attack |

Creature **Evasion** adds its printed Boons or Banes to your attack. **Threat** adds
its printed Boons or Banes to your defense against that creature's attack. These
use the ordinary dice rules; do not add them numerically to the total.

If you control a summon, roll that creature's printed attributes. Its player profile
already presents attack outcomes in the correct direction. Your hero's own Brawn
or Reason does not replace the summon’s value.

For NPC-only actions, a player or the DA assuming the player role rolls. For an
NPC attack against another NPC, roll the defender’s printed attribute and read
the attacker’s defense-outcome table. For consequential healing or another task,
roll the acting NPC’s attribute. Make one roll; handling dice does not transfer
control of the NPC. Off-screen events can use DA judgment.

## Damage and resistance

Damage comes from the chosen outcome, not a weapon damage die. Your attribute has
already affected the roll; do not add it again to damage. Apply each matching
resistance after determining the outcome. **Armor DR is physical resistance.**

Use the highest applicable resistance of each type, to a maximum of 3. Two sources
of physical resistance 2 do not give 4. Physical resistance 2 and Fire resistance 1
can apply together because they protect against different types.

An attack that deals damage has a minimum of **1 total damage** after reductions
if any of its original damage survives immunity. Damage from conditions, falls,
and collisions can be reduced to 0.

> **Example — steel and flame.** An attack deals 3 physical and 1 fire damage.
> Physical resistance 2 reduces the physical portion to 1. Fire resistance 1 removes
> the fire portion. Take 1 total damage, not one of each type. If both portions had
> been reduced to zero by resistance, the attack would still deal 1 total damage.

Physical includes impacts, sonic force and supernatural force when the attack says
physical. Fire, Cold and Lightning have separate resistances. Life resistance reduces magical
healing and potions, but not First Aid or overnight recovery.

### Damage and condition immunities

Use the immunities listed for the creature or granted by an effect. **Damage
immunity** removes the named damage type from the event before weakness or
resistance. If immunity removes all of the damage, the event deals **0 HP damage**.
The rest of the outcome still applies unless its rules require damage or prevent
the effect. **Condition immunity** prevents the named condition from applying.

Damage immunities can name **Physical, Fire, Cold, Lightning, Poison, Life,
Radiant, Mental,** or **Force**. Condition immunities name a specific condition.
The bestiary includes immunity to **Asleep, Bleeding, Blinded, Frightened,** and
**Poisoned**. A creature or effect can explicitly name another condition.

Against Fire damage immunity, a hit for 2 Physical and 3 Fire loses its Fire
damage. If Physical resistance reduces the remaining damage to 0, the hit still
deals 1 total damage.

> **Example — Burning 2.** Fire resistance 3 reduces the tick to 0 damage, as
> does Fire damage immunity. In both cases Burning drops to 1 at turn end.
> A creature immune to Burning never gains the condition, and a separate Fire
> hit can still damage it.

Same-kind numerical bonuses do not add together unless explicitly stated. Conditions
with meaningful ratings can add; binary Prone cannot. Boons and Banes use their own
stacking rules. **Weakness X** adds X to its matching damage component before
resistance, once per event. Use the highest value of each type, normally capped
at 3. It cannot add a damage type absent from the attack. Special vulnerabilities
use their printed procedure. Fire Weakness 2 turns 3 fire damage into 5 before
resistance; it adds nothing to a purely physical attack.

## Shields and guarded positions

Defend is a universal Maneuver that gives 1 Boon to defenses until the start of your
next turn. Repeating Defend does not increase that same benefit.

When the DA judges your held shield can block an attack against you, spend your
Reaction before the roll to Shield Block. While holding the shield, gain 1 Boon
to defenses against blockable attacks until the start of your next turn. If the
attacker rolls instead, apply 1 Bane to the attack roll. Most ordinary physical
attacks can be blocked. Combine Defend and Shield Block as separate sources.

## Opportunity attacks

Leaving an enemy's melee reach voluntarily, including by crawling, can provoke.
Casting beside an enemy, standing, stowing an item, or retrieving one can also
provoke. Spend your Reaction to make **Basic Melee**
with a held melee weapon or **Basic Unarmed** with a free hand. A DA creature uses
its bestiary Basic Melee. Resolve the attack **at the start of the provoking action**,
before the original action takes effect.

Then continue the original action if its actor is capable. Damage alone does not
cancel it. Recheck targets and range before continuing. At 0 HP, an actor must regain HP before they can act again. Commit the action on declaration;
if interrupted permanently, that action is spent. Pay the printed cost when the action continues into resolution. An unspent potion is not drunk
by an interrupted character who can no longer act.

Drawing a weapon as part of attacking adds no separate action. Dropping an item is
free. Stowing or picking up an item costs a Maneuver. Forced movement never provokes.
An ability can explicitly allow movement without provoking.

> **Example — a spell under pressure.** Vaelis begins casting beside an armed foe.
> The foe spends its Reaction on Basic Melee. Vaelis makes the required defense and
> loses HP. Vaelis can still act, so she checks her targets again, pays the
> spell's SP cost and resolves it. If the attack drops her to 0 HP, she spends
> the action she declared and keeps the SP.

## Distance, space and cover

All distances use **squares**. A square is the useful unit for your map; it does not
require a fixed conversion into feet or meters. Normal ground costs 1 movement per
square and difficult ground costs 2. While Prone, crawl for 2 movement per normal
square or 3 per difficult square. Straight and diagonal steps cost the same.
Standing costs 2 movement.

You can cross an occupied square if its occupant is Prone. Pay the higher of 2
movement or your usual cost to enter it, and finish in a free square. An ability
that moves you without provoking still respects terrain, occupied spaces and legal
endpoints unless it explicitly says otherwise.

A sight-required target must be visible to you or located by an explicit
alternative-sense targeting grant. An attack needs a usable path to its target.
The DA judges whether an obstruction protects the target from that attack.
**Partial cover** gives the attacker **1 Bane**. **Heavy cover** gives the
attacker **3 Banes** and still leaves a narrow attack path, as through a thicket.
If you roll defense, take **1 Boon** for partial cover or **3 Boons** for heavy
cover instead. Apply cover once, using the usual Boon and Bane rules. A barrier
that blocks the path prevents the attack.

For a player area attack, choose the printed range, shape, inclusion and exclusions.
Roll once using the **worst applicable net Boon/Bane situation** among its targets.
Use that result for all targets; apply their resistances individually. When an NPC
area attack affects several players, each player makes their own defense roll.

## Forced movement

- **Push X** moves the target up to X squares directly away from the source.
- **Pull X** moves the target up to X squares directly toward the source.
- **Slide X** moves the target up to X squares in any direction, including vertically.

If you use the effect, choose the Slide path or where to stop a Push or Pull.
Follow any restrictions printed in the effect. A Push or Pull changes elevation
only if its effect allows it. A creature thrown by an ability follows that ability's
directions. You can stop before using the full distance. Collision damage occurs
only if the target actually hits something.

Apply **Stability** once to the initial target, reducing the available forced
movement to a minimum of 0. Stability is normally 0. Use the highest explicit
grant, to a maximum of 3.

Spend the entered square's terrain cost from the movement budget. If any positive
budget remains, the target enters the final square even if its cost exceeds that
budget, then stops. For example, push 1 can enter one difficult square and stop.
Stability does not reduce Prone, conditions, voluntary movement, projectile range,
obstacle progress or the reduction of a grapple.

When a moving creature hits a movable creature or object, they move together on
what remains of the original movement allowance. On each new impact, everyone in
the group and whatever it strikes take **physical damage** equal to the movement
remaining at contact. Creatures and objects with HP each apply their own damage
defenses. For an object without HP, the DA decides how the
impact affects it. A movable object that breaks drops out of the group.
Resolve damage before subtracting a new creature's Stability, once per creature
for that movement. Continued contact deals no further damage.

A fixed barrier stops the group even if it breaks. Add 1 to the damage dealt to
each group member and the barrier before resistance. After placing the group,
only the original mover bounces one square opposite the impact. If that square
is blocked, the mover stays in place without another collision or damage.

> **Example — A third creature joins.** Two creatures moving together hit a third
> with 3 squares left. Each takes 3 damage before armor. The new creature has
> Stability 2, so the whole group has 1 square left to move.

> **Crowded collisions.** Moving groups must finish in separate legal spaces.
> If everyone cannot fit, stop at the last position where they can; the DA decides
> the arrangement. Placement cannot pass through walls or grant extra forward
> movement.

## Grappling and capture

Grappling requires a learned ability; it is not automatically granted with Basic Melee.
Grappled prevents movement. At ratings 1, 2 and 3, retain respectively two, one or
none of Main Action, Maneuver and Reaction, chosen at turn start. The grappler is
restricted by their own contribution as well. Multiple grapplers' contributions add
on the target. Attacks against a Grappled target gain Boons equal to its rating.

If you still have a Main Action, Force can reduce your grapple by 1/2/3. At
Grappled 3 or higher, you can escape only if a grappler releases you or an outside
intervention breaks the hold. For example, an ally can move the grappler out of
reach or knock them unconscious. A grappler can freely release their own
contribution. A maintained grapple lasts until the hold ends.

Attacks are lethal by default. An ability such as Pinning Strike can give you a
nonlethal option. Declare that option before rolling and follow the ability's
printed outcome. You can also take someone alive by securing their surrender,
making them helpless, or holding them with a grapple.

With a free hand and suitable [restraints](../../equipment/restraints.md), spend a
Maneuver to cuff an adjacent creature that has surrendered, is helpless, or is
Grappled 3 or higher. Once it is cuffed, a grappler can release their hold. The
restraints bind the limbs they enclose until opened or escaped. Return to ordinary
narration when the captive is secured and the immediate fight is over.

> An ally has knocked a guard unconscious with a nonlethal Pinning Strike. You
> move beside the guard and spend a Maneuver to cuff their wrists. When the guard
> wakes, the cuffs still bind their hands.

## Ending a fight

A fight ends when the immediate opposition is resolved, not because everyone decides
to ignore an active death roll. Resolve Dying before leaving combat timing. When it
is safe to pause and companions can attend to an ordinary fire or similar immediate
hazard, settle that hazard as the scene allows. Other conditions remain until their
own removal, expiry or remedy. Safe overnight rest restores HP and SP; it does not erase scars, refund Grit,
cure every condition or restore the dead. A brief pause gives no recovery.

records.title: Equipment and Recipes
records.markdown:
# Equipment and Recipes

A coil of rope is easy to overlook until someone is hanging above a ravine. Choose
equipment for the journey you expect, leave room for what you might find, and know
which hand will reach your potion when the fight goes badly.

## Coins and trade

HOL uses one currency: **coins**. A listed price buys the described ordinary item or
full supply. Choose armor that matches the training you’ve learned.

Useful intact gear sells for **half its listed value**, rounded down, or trades at
**full value** with a willing trader. A 12-coin weapon sells for 6 or trades for
12 coins of goods. Pay any shortfall in coins; excess trade value is not cash change.
A merchant does not have unlimited stock or an obligation to buy everything you make.

## Armor and training

Choose a suit of armor to match your training and acquire it with your other equipment. Its resistance applies only while worn and with the matching learned training.

| Training | Requirement | DP | Physical resistance |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| [Armored Training I](../../disciplines/armor.md) | Study Armor | 1 | Light: 1 |
| Armored Training II | Armored Training I | 2 | Medium: 2 |
| Armored Training III | Armored Training II | 2 | Heavy: 3 |

All three may be learned at level 0. Each new step lets you use its armor category as well as any you learned earlier. Use the highest applicable resistance, never their sum. Attacks deal at least 1 damage after resistance if any damaging component survives immunity.

## Bulk and hands

Record each carried item's **Bulk**. Most individual equipment entries and supply
bundles use 1 Bulk; the entry tells you otherwise. A pack adds its own Bulk and does
not erase its contents. Capacity is 10 + 3 × Brawn. Each Bulk above capacity reduces
Speed by 1, to a minimum of 0.

A single compatible weapon serves all the attacks that can use it. Ordinary weapon
appearance changes no mechanics. A flaming melee weapon can add its printed fire
effect to a compatible attack; it cannot become a ranged weapon simply because
you chose a ranged card.

Track occupied hands. Healing requires a free hand. A bow, two-handed weapon, or
weapon-and-shield combination leaves none. Drawing for an attack is part of that
attack, dropping is free, and proper stowing or picking up costs a Maneuver. There
is no automatic free grip-change exception.

## Inventory dice

A supply bundle has an inventory die instead of a counted number of uses. After
using it, roll that die. On a **1**, reduce it one step. On any other result it stays
where it is. The use you just completed still works.

**d20 → d12 → d10 → d8 → d6 → d4 → out**

Check at the interval printed on the supply: ammunition when used, food by its
person-day rule, lighting by its hour, and so on. A d4 healing bottle has a one-in-four
chance of becoming empty after each use. It is not a promise of four doses.

> **Example — the last swallow.** You drink a lesser healing bottle and restore its
> 6 HP, reduced by Life resistance if applicable. Then roll its d4 inventory die.
> A 1 empties the bottle; you still received that healing. At full HP the bottle
> cannot heal beyond your maximum.

Recipes raise an existing supply by their permitted number of steps, up to the
recipe's cap. A store refill uses the listed policy. Do not turn unknown leftovers
into additional full bottles by splitting them among containers.

## Special equipment and understanding

A special item adds only the effects it prints: damage, resistance, an ability or
another explicit benefit. Apply normal nonstacking rules to matching numerical
bonuses. Different damage-type resistances can coexist; use the highest of each.

The item states whether understanding is required. Identification abilities reveal
different kinds of information. Knowing a recipe is a separate permission from
knowing what an item does. The recipe section lists tools, materials, time and what
the crafting result produces; none of those are supplied by the recipe's name alone.

### Items that change attributes

**Add a modifier.** For each attribute, add the highest applicable item bonus
and subtract the largest applicable item penalty. Published item modifiers range
from −2 to +2. Your effective attribute can go beyond the creation range.

**Cursed penalties.** If a cursed item penalizes an attribute, apply the largest
applicable item penalty and ignore item bonuses to that attribute while the curse
applies.

**Set a value.** If an item sets an attribute to a specific value, use that exact
value while the item applies. It replaces your base value and every bonus and
penalty to that attribute. You can use one item that sets a given attribute at a
time. Apply any exception printed on a curse card, such as suppressing item bonuses
or taking precedence over other effects.

> With Brawn +1 and item bonuses of +2 and +1, your effective Brawn is +3. A cursed
> item with a −1 Brawn penalty suppresses both bonuses and brings your Brawn to 0.
> An item that sets Brawn to +3 gives you exactly +3 unless the curse overrides it.
